script.opening: “Hi, thanks. I’ve had bad indigestion for a few months and I’ve been taking Gaviscon and Rennies. And I’ve been a bit down, so I got some St John’s wort online. I just suddenly thought — is that alright with my HIV tablets? And could I have something stronger for my stomach?”

facts.text: “Diagnosed nine years ago. I take Biktarvy, one tablet every morning with breakfast. Never miss it. The clinic says I’m undetectable.” Clinic every 6 months; next appointment in 3 months.
“I take Gaviscon Advance and a couple of Rennies most mornings — usually with my breakfast and my Biktarvy, because that’s when it’s bad. Sometimes again at night.”
“I’ve been taking it six weeks, one tablet twice a day. I haven’t told the clinic.” No other herbal or recreational drugs. Alcohol about 14 units a week, mostly wine at weekends. Non-smoker.

“Burning in the upper tummy and up into my chest after meals, worse lying down. Three months.” If asked: no difficulty swallowing, no vomiting, no weight loss (weight steady), no black stools or blood, appetite fine. No family history of stomach or oesophageal cancer. Coffee four cups a day. Eats late.
No other prescribed medicines. Takes ibuprofen occasionally for his back — “maybe once a week”.

If asked: “Low for about two months. Not sleeping great, less interested in things, tired.” If asked about self-harm: “No, never — nothing like that. I’ve got a lot to live for.” No previous depression.

If asked what is behind the low mood, or about relationships: “I’ve met someone — Sarah — three months ago. I haven’t told her. Last time I told someone, my ex-wife, she told half our friends. I keep putting off… you know, being intimate. I’m terrified she’ll leave.”
If U=U is mentioned: “So I really can’t pass it on? Even without condoms? Do I legally have to tell her?”
If asked whether he has any other worries: “The receptionist here lives on my street. Can she see my notes?”
Happy for the GP to write to the HIV clinic once confidentiality is explained.

Pleasant, practical, a bit embarrassed. You want the medicines question answered quickly. Only mention Sarah if the doctor explores the low mood (what is going on in your life, what is getting you down). If the doctor asks about mood in a box-ticking way, say “just work stress”. If the doctor explains U=U clearly, become emotional and relieved. If the doctor tells you that you must tell Sarah before anything else, become defensive.

data.kind: HIV clinic letter — bloods 3 months ago

ice.ideas: The antacids and herbal remedy are “natural” and probably harmless; indigestion may be from stress.
ice.concerns: That he has damaged his HIV control; telling Sarah and being rejected; people finding out (receptionist).
ice.expectations: A yes or no about his remedies and a stronger indigestion medicine.

cues: “I’ve been a bit down” — mentioned in passing as the reason for St John’s wort.
“I haven’t told the clinic” — said with embarrassment.
Looks away when asked if anything else is going on.

checkpoints.text: Takes a full drug history including timing, over-the-counter and herbal products, and recreational drugs and alcohol
Assesses dyspepsia for alarm features (weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting, GI bleeding, anaemia, age) and contributing factors (NSAIDs, alcohol, caffeine, late meals)
Explores the low mood — duration, impact, cause — and assesses risk of self-harm; elicits the disclosure worry

Identifies and explains the interactions — stop St John’s wort (risk of viral rebound and resistance); separate antacids from Biktarvy (at least 2 hours before) — and checks using the Liverpool HIV interactions resource or the HIV clinic
Manages dyspepsia safely — lifestyle advice, stop ibuprofen, a PPI that does not interact with his regimen, H. pylori test-and-treat with correct timing — and safety-nets for alarm features

Offers mood management that is safe with antiretrovirals (talking therapy, HIV clinic psychology, an interaction-checked antidepressant if needed), arranges review and writes to the HIV clinic with consent
Explains U=U accurately and supports him with disclosure without pressure, signposting peer support
Responds to the confidentiality worry honestly — explains records access, audit and how to raise concerns — and is non-judgemental about the unreported remedies

worked.txt: “When exactly do you take the Gaviscon and Rennies in relation to your Biktarvy? Anything else — herbal, online, from the gym?”
“St John’s wort speeds up how your body clears some HIV medicines, so levels can drop. That can let the virus come back and become resistant. I’d stop it today.”

“Indigestion remedies with calcium, magnesium or aluminium stop Biktarvy being absorbed properly. Take your Biktarvy at least 2 hours before them — or better, let’s treat the indigestion another way.”
“You mentioned feeling down — what do you think is behind it?”
“Your viral load has been undetectable for years. That means you cannot pass HIV on through sex. That’s well established.”
“Staff only access records when they need to for their job, and access is logged. If you’d like, we can review who has seen your record and restrict it.”

f.learning: Many people with HIV take over-the-counter and herbal products without telling their clinic. Always take a full drug history and check interactions (the Liverpool HIV Drug Interactions website is the standard resource; the HIV clinic pharmacist can advise). St John’s wort induces drug-metabolising enzymes and transporters and must not be taken with Biktarvy and many other antiretrovirals. Polyvalent cations (aluminium, magnesium, calcium, iron) chelate integrase inhibitors: take Biktarvy at least 2 hours before antacids. PPIs are compatible with Biktarvy but contraindicated with rilpivirine and atazanavir — check the regimen. Low mood is common in people living with HIV and is often linked to stigma and disclosure. U=U (undetectable = untransmittable): a person with a sustained undetectable viral load cannot transmit HIV sexually. In England and Wales criminal cases concern actual transmission; being on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load means sexual transmission will not occur. Support disclosure decisions; reassure about confidentiality; share information with the HIV clinic with consent.

Exact timing of antacids and Biktarvy; St John’s wort; NSAIDs, alcohol; alarm features.
Explore cause; risk assessment; elicit the relationship and disclosure fear.
Stop St John’s wort; antacid timing; PPI plus H. pylori test; mood support safe with ART; check interactions; letter to clinic.

wordPics.clearPass: Takes a precise drug history, identifies both interactions and explains them clearly with a practical plan, manages dyspepsia safely with alarm features screened, explores the low mood to uncover the disclosure fear, explains U=U accurately and supportively, addresses the confidentiality worry honestly, and liaises with the HIV clinic with consent.
wordPics.pass: Identifies the St John’s wort interaction and antacid timing, treats dyspepsia sensibly and assesses mood and risk; the disclosure issue or confidentiality worry is handled more briefly.
wordPics.fail: Identifies one interaction only, or prescribes without checking interactions; mood assessed superficially; misses the relationship and disclosure concern.
wordPics.clearFail: Reassures that herbal remedies and antacids are fine; prescribes an interacting medicine; judgemental about HIV or disclosure; gives inaccurate transmission or legal information.

avoid.dont: “Herbal remedies are natural, so they won’t do any harm.”
avoid.instead: “St John’s wort can lower the levels of your HIV medicine — that’s why I’d stop it.”
avoid.why: Enzyme induction can cause virological failure and resistance.

avoid.dont: “You have to tell her before you sleep with her — it’s the law.”
avoid.instead: “With an undetectable viral load you can’t pass HIV on through sex. When and how you tell Sarah is your decision, and there’s support to help.”
avoid.why: Inaccurate and stigmatising; U=U is established.

avoid.instead: “Omeprazole is fine with Biktarvy — I’ll double-check with the interaction checker and let your clinic know.”
avoid.why: PPIs interact with some antiretrovirals; always check the specific regimen.

model.text: Hello Tom, I’m Dr Evans. You’ve got questions about indigestion remedies and your HIV medicines — tell me more.
Gaviscon and Rennies for three months, and St John’s wort for six weeks because I’ve been down. Is that okay with Biktarvy? And can I have something stronger?
Thank you for asking — it’s really sensible. When do you take the antacids compared with your Biktarvy? And anything else — other herbal remedies, painkillers, anything from online or the gym?
model.why: Precise timing and full drug history

model.text: With breakfast, same time as Biktarvy. Ibuprofen sometimes for my back. Nothing else.
Any difficulty swallowing, vomiting, weight loss, black stools or blood? How much alcohol and coffee?
None of those. Fourteen units a week, four coffees a day, I eat late.
You mentioned feeling down. How long, and what do you think is behind it?
Couple of months. I’ve met someone — Sarah. I haven’t told her about my HIV. Last time, my ex-wife told our friends. I’m scared she’ll leave.
That sounds really hard to carry. Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or that life isn’t worth living?

Let’s take the medicines first. St John’s wort speeds up how your body clears Biktarvy, so levels can fall, which can let the virus come back and become resistant. Please stop it today. The antacids stick to Biktarvy and stop it being absorbed — if you need one, take Biktarvy at least 2 hours before. Better still, a medicine like omeprazole works well with Biktarvy; I’ll confirm on the HIV interactions checker before I prescribe.
model.why: Explains both interactions and a safe alternative

model.text: I had no idea. Have I messed up my HIV?

Very unlikely, but it’s worth a viral load test in the next few weeks to be sure — I’ll ask your clinic. With your consent I’ll write to them about all of this. We’ll also do a breath or stool test for a stomach bug called H. pylori, which needs you off omeprazole for 2 weeks, so we’ll do that first. Cutting down on late meals, coffee and ibuprofen will help too.
model.why: Viral load check, liaison with clinic, H. pylori timing, lifestyle

model.text: About Sarah — your viral load has been undetectable for years. That means you cannot pass HIV on through sex. It’s called U=U. When and how you tell her is your choice, and the clinic’s health advisers and groups like Positively UK can help you plan it.
model.why: Accurate U=U and supportive approach to disclosure

model.text: (emotional) I didn’t really believe that. And — the receptionist lives on my street. Can she see my notes?

Staff only access records when needed for their job, and every access is logged. If you’d like, we can check who has looked at your record and add extra restrictions. For your mood, talking therapy or the clinic psychologist would be a good start, and if we consider an antidepressant I’ll pick one that’s safe with Biktarvy. Let’s speak again in 4 weeks — sooner if things get worse or you develop swallowing problems, vomiting or black stools.
model.why: Honest confidentiality reassurance, mood plan and safety-net

model.text: Thank you. That’s a weight off.

knowledge.guideline: BHIVA guidelines for the treatment of HIV-1-positive adults with antiretroviral therapy (2022) · University of Liverpool HIV Drug Interactions checker (current) · Biktarvy Summary of Product Characteristics (EMC, current) · NICE CG184 Dyspepsia and GORD in adults (2014, updated 2019) · NICE NG222 Depression in adults (2022) · BHIVA/BASHH position on U=U
knowledge.summary: Antiretroviral therapy interacts with many common medicines and herbal products. Always check, using the Liverpool resource or the HIV clinic. A sustained undetectable viral load means HIV cannot be transmitted sexually (U=U).

points.t: Induces CYP3A, UGT1A1 and P-glycoprotein, lowering levels of bictegravir and tenofovir alafenamide (and many other antiretrovirals). Co-administration must be avoided; check viral load if exposure has occurred.

Aluminium, magnesium, calcium and iron reduce integrase inhibitor absorption. For Biktarvy, take at least 2 hours before (or 6 hours after) aluminium/magnesium antacids; calcium or iron supplements can be taken together with food. Check the SmPC for the exact advice.
PPIs and H2 blockers are compatible with Biktarvy, but PPIs are contraindicated with rilpivirine and reduce atazanavir. Always check the specific regimen.
Screen for alarm features; under 55 without alarm features: lifestyle changes, review NSAIDs, full-dose PPI for 4 weeks or H. pylori test-and-treat (2 weeks off PPI before testing).

Depression is more common in people living with HIV. Offer psychological therapy; if an antidepressant is needed, check interactions (sertraline and citalopram are often suitable with integrase-based regimens).
People with HIV on treatment with a sustained undetectable viral load (under 200 copies/mL) do not transmit HIV sexually. Endorsed by BHIVA and BASHH.

There is no general legal duty to disclose HIV status. In England and Wales, prosecutions concern actual transmission where the person was reckless or intentional; with an undetectable viral load, sexual transmission does not occur. Support the person to decide about disclosure.
GP and HIV clinic share responsibility: record antiretrovirals on the GP system as hospital-prescribed to trigger interaction alerts, and communicate changes.

social.t: Previous breaches by an ex-partner and fear of rejection are common drivers of low mood. Peer support helps.

legal.t: Data Protection Act 2018 / UK GDPR: access to records only for a legitimate purpose; access is auditable. Patients can ask for an access audit.

professional.t: Share information with the HIV clinic with consent for direct care. Do not disclose HIV status to partners without consent; with an undetectable viral load there is no risk that could justify it.

community.t: Positively UK (peer support), Terrence Higgins Trust (THT Direct), NAM aidsmap, HIV clinic health advisers and psychology.

redFlags: Dysphagia, vomiting, weight loss, GI bleeding, anaemia
Missed antiretroviral doses or viral rebound
psychosocial: New relationship and fear of disclosure
ice: Concern: damaged HIV control; rejection; being found out
Expectation: yes/no answer and a stronger medicine

playbook.diagnosis: Uncomplicated dyspepsia; clinically significant interactions (St John’s wort, cation antacids with bictegravir); mild–moderate low mood linked to disclosure fears; HIV well controlled.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “St John’s wort can make your HIV tablets work less well, and indigestion remedies can stop them being absorbed. Let’s stop the herbal tablet and treat the indigestion in a way that doesn’t clash.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought these were harmless — lots of people do. You were right to ask. And the low mood seems to be about Sarah, which we can help with.”
management.psychosocial: U=U explained; disclosure support; confidentiality audit offered; peer support.
sharedPlan: Stop St John’s wort today; viral load check via clinic
Biktarvy at least 2 hours before any antacid; omeprazole after interaction check
H. pylori test after 2 weeks off PPI; lifestyle; stop ibuprofen
Talking therapy/clinic psychology; letter to HIV clinic with consent
safetyNet: Swallowing difficulty, vomiting, black stools, weight loss → contact promptly
Worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm → same-day contact, 111, Samaritans 116 123

pitfalls.intro: He asks two simple questions. The marks are in the drug history, the hidden relationship, and getting U=U right.

items.fail: Prescribing a PPI and saying “carry on with the rest”.
items.why: St John’s wort risks viral rebound and resistance.
items.fix: Stop it, explain why, and check viral load.

items.fail: Not asking when antacids are taken.
items.why: Taking them with Biktarvy reduces absorption.
items.fix: Ask exact timing and advise separation.

items.fail: Treating the low mood as a tick-box.
items.why: The cause — fear of disclosure — is what he needs help with.

items.fail: Telling him he must disclose by law, or that condoms are essential.
items.fix: Explain U=U and offer disclosure support.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Follows “I’ve been a bit down”, “I haven’t told the clinic” and his looking away when asked if anything else is going on.
Idea (remedies natural and harmless; stress indigestion); concern (damaged HIV control, Sarah’s rejection, people finding out); expectation (yes/no and a stronger medicine).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — That he has damaged his HIV control; telling Sarah and being rejected; people finding out (receptionist) — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
